## RoboMIND: multi-embodiment under one protocol

RoboMIND's paper reports 107,000 successful trajectories totaling 305.5 interaction hours across 479 tasks and 96 object classes. The cohort mixes real-world and simulated demonstrations for four embodiments, a Franka Emika Panda, a UR5e, an AgileX dual-arm robot and a humanoid with dual dexterous hands, under one collection platform and standardized protocol. It releases 5,000 real-world failure demonstrations with annotated causes and a digital twin of its tasks in Isaac Sim <Cite id="robomind-2024" />.

RoboMIND 2.0 (December 2025) reports over 310K dual-arm trajectories from six embodiments and 739 tasks, including 12K tactile-enhanced episodes and 20K mobile manipulation trajectories <Cite id="robomind-2-2025" />. The [public dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/x-humanoid-robomind/RoboMIND) shows an Apache-2.0 tag but makes users accept access conditions before downloading, so check the terms before commercial use <Cite id="robomind-dataset-card" />.

## How to read dataset claims

Hours compare better than episodes. DROID averages about 17 seconds per trajectory and AgiBot World Beta about 11, so a large episode count can hide less interaction than fewer long tasks ([the data bottleneck](/data-hardware/data-bottleneck)). The 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge supplies 10,000 teleoperated demonstrations totaling 1,200+ hours <Cite id="behavior-challenge-2025" />, and the synthetic InternData-A1 holds over 630k trajectories and 7,433 hours <Cite id="interndata-a1-2025" />.

Modalities differ as much as size. RH20T records visual, force, audio and action data in over 110,000 contact-rich sequences <Cite id="rh20t-2023" />. Humanoid Everyday adds depth, LiDAR and tactile streams to 10.3k humanoid trajectories across 260 tasks, with a cloud evaluation platform <Cite id="humanoid-everyday-2025" />. Scaling work finds task diversity worth more than per-task demonstration count, and multi-embodiment pretraining optional given high-quality single-embodiment data <Cite id="diversity-scaling-2025" />.

Hand-object datasets make contact supervision explicit. ContactDB uses thermal imaging to record grasp-contact maps <Cite id="contactdb-2019" />; ContactPose pairs contact with hand pose, object pose and RGB-D images <Cite id="contactpose-2020" />. DexYCB benchmarks hand and object pose estimation and safe robot grasps for human-to-robot handover <Cite id="dexycb-2021" />.

HOI4D supplies egocentric RGB-D video with hand-pose, object-pose and action annotations <Cite id="hoi4d-2022" />. OakInk connects object affordances to recorded human interactions and transfers those interactions to virtual counterparts <Cite id="oakink-2022" />.

Object models supply another kind of supervision. ShapeNet organizes CAD models by semantic category and records attributes such as alignment and size <Cite id="shapenet-2015" />. PartNet adds detailed hierarchical part labels <Cite id="partnet-2018" />; ABC retains explicitly parameterized curves and surfaces for geometric ground truth <Cite id="abc-models-2018" />. The YCB set pairs physical everyday objects with scans, physical properties, geometric models and example manipulation protocols <Cite id="ycb-models-2015" />.

## Releases since 2025

RoboCOIN offers over 180,000 bimanual demonstrations from 15 platforms and 421 tasks <Cite id="robocoin-2025" />. Scale AI and Hugging Face's FineART (September 2026) has 1,718 hours of bimanual teleoperation in 40,543 episodes, with 533,913 human-labelled subtasks across 151 tasks <Cite id="fineart-2026" />. SmolVLA trained on fewer than 30k episodes, all from community-contributed datasets <Cite id="smolvla-2025" />. The community-built AXIS holds 50K+ trajectories over 207 tasks, and continual pretraining on it raised π0.5's overall success rate by 5.8% <Cite id="axis-2026" />.

In simulation, RoboCasa365 offers 365 tasks across 2,500 kitchens, with over 600 hours of human and over 1,600 hours of synthetic demonstrations <Cite id="robocasa365-2026" />.

## From dataset headline to training contract

A useful dataset is legal for the intended deployment, consistent in actions, units, frames and rates, complete for the claimed tasks, scenes and embodiments, and downloadable as versioned episodes traceable to a release. Datasheets for Datasets asks every dataset to document its motivation, composition, collection process and recommended uses <Cite id="datasheets-for-datasets-2018" />. LeRobot's format moved to multi-episode files in 2025, after one file per episode hit file-system limits at millions of episodes <Cite id="lerobot-dataset-v3-2025" />.

Mixing datasets needs a canonical observation and action schema, one adapter per source and source labels kept through training, so positive transfer can be told apart from one corpus dominating <Cite id="open-x-embodiment-2023" /> <Cite id="octo-2024" /> <Cite id="remix-2024" />. The [robot-learning stack](/data-hardware/robot-learning-stack) supplies the versioned artifacts, and the [robot-learning roadmap](/manipulation/robot-learning-roadmap) places dataset selection in a broader program.

Isaac Lab wraps GPU simulation, sensors, task definitions and batched environments into a robot-learning workflow <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />. A learned world model estimates transitions from observations and actions, often in a latent or video space, and trades parameter error for dataset and generalization error. <span id="what-each-representation-costs-to-run" />
## A latent planner needs seconds per action, a video planner minutes

The table compares the query cost of four representations on one machine; the FLOP row is a derived order-of-magnitude estimate. For a physics baseline, Isaac Gym steps thousands of environments in parallel on one GPU and trained robot tasks 2 to 3 orders of magnitude faster than CPU-simulator pipelines <Cite id="isaac-gym-2021" />.

<WorldModelCostTable className="my-6" />

As the decode reference, Llama 3 8B <Cite id="llama-3-2024" /> holds about 16 GB of fp16 weights. Its 32 layers and 8 grouped-query key-value heads <Cite id="llama-3-herd-2024" /> give a KV cache of about 128 KB per token.

In the latent column, V-JEPA 2-AC's cross-entropy planner takes about 16 seconds per action with 800 samples over 10 iterations. A Cosmos video planner took about 4 minutes with 80 samples, roughly 15x slower, and both looked one step ahead <Cite id="vjepa2-2025" />. LeWorldModel plans up to 48x faster than foundation-model world models <Cite id="leworldmodel-2026" />.

<WorldModelOutputTimes className="my-6" />

## Clip generators run far slower than interactive world models

In the costlier video column, Cosmos Predict1 spans diffusion models at 7B to 14B and autoregressive models at 4B to 13B <Cite id="cosmos-predict-2025" />. NVIDIA measured Predict2's 14B Video2World at 56 GB of VRAM and about 85 seconds per 480p clip on a GB200, over 30 minutes on a DGX Spark <Cite id="cosmos-predict2-perf-2025" />. The Predict1 14B card lists over 80 GB for a five-second 1280x704 clip with the prompt upsampler offloaded <Cite id="cosmos-1-diffusion-14b-card-2025" />. Such offline clip generators cannot serve as 24 fps runtimes, and a policy calling one per action step inherits their latency.

DeepMind reports that Genie 3 runs at 24 fps and 720p <Cite id="genie-3-2025" />, and the Interactive World Simulator holds 15 FPS for over 10 minutes on one RTX 4090 <Cite id="interactive-world-simulator-2026" />. DreamZero controls a robot at 7 Hz from a 14B video model <Cite id="dreamzero-2026" />.

## Gaussian splats render in milliseconds but carry no dynamics

3D Gaussian Splatting renders rasterizable primitives in tens of milliseconds or less per frame, with no weights or tokens, and stores the scene as an asset of 1 to 5 million Gaussians <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />. A splat shows what a view looks like; physics must say what an action does.

<Image id="gaussian-splatting-garden-2023" />

<span id="where-physics-remains-difficult-to-replace" />
## Physics stays ahead for untried actions and checkable safety limits

Planning, as in [model-based RL](/world-models/model-based-robot-learning/), queries actions the dataset did not take. A physics engine integrates them while its modeled regime holds; a learned model must extrapolate, and a planner can exploit its errors by picking actions with spuriously high predicted reward. Across six video generators, physical understanding was "severely limited, and unrelated to visual realism" <Cite id="physics-iq-2025" />. Safety constraints also favor explicit state: joint limits, collision geometry, force bounds and signed distances can be checked directly, while a predicted video may imply a collision without the quantity a monitor needs.

<PlannerExploit className="my-6" />

<span id="where-learning-has-the-advantage" />
## Learning captures appearance and contact that are costly to model

A learned visual model can absorb from video the textures, reflections, cables and clutter that are expensive to render; deformable contacts, unmodeled actuators and wear also resist parameterization. Robotic World Model aims a neural simulator at policy optimization <Cite id="robotic-world-model-2025" />, and RoboWorld at policy evaluation, with task-progress scoring and rankings validated against real robots <Cite id="roboworld-2026" />.

<span id="three-hybrid-patterns" />
## Four hybrid patterns

### Learn appearance, keep dynamics

Real-to-sim systems reconstruct a scene's appearance and keep a physics engine for motion and contact, as RoboGSim does with Gaussian splatting <Cite id="robogsim-2024" />. SplatSim's splat-rendered simulator gave zero-shot RGB policies 86.25% success, against 97.5% when trained on real data <Cite id="splatsim-2024" />. The pattern suits rigid-body tasks and is weaker for friction or tool compliance. PhysTwin extends it to deformables, building spring-mass twins of ropes, stuffed animals, cloth and delivery packages from videos and rendering them with Gaussian splats <Cite id="phystwin-2025" />. A separate soft-body evaluation framework reconstructs video-based twins and uses splat-rendered rollouts to assess policies for plush-toy packing and rope routing <Cite id="softbody-splat-eval-2025" />.

### Generate content, keep the engine

[Generative simulation](/world-models/generative-sim/) uses models to author objects, layouts, tasks and assets inside a physics engine, so the generator supplies coverage while the engine keeps contact causal. RoboCasa supplies large-scale everyday manipulation environments <Cite id="robocasa-2024" />, and RoboCasa365 extends it to training and benchmarking generalist robots <Cite id="robocasa365-2026" />.

### Learn residual dynamics

Residual models start from explicit dynamics and learn the measured difference, such as actuator delay or contact impulses. With a named error to fit, this is the most conservative hybrid <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />. ASAP trains a delta action model on real Unitree G1 data and beats system-identification, domain-randomization and delta-dynamics baselines on tracking error <Cite id="asap-2025" />. A residual fitted to nominal walking may still fail on a fall.

### Pretrain in simulation, adapt dynamics on hardware

SimDist trains a world model on simulated experience, then on real data updates only the latent dynamics, keeping the encoder, reward model and value function. Its authors say this reduces adaptation to supervised system identification, and it kept improving with experience on contact-rich manipulation and quadruped locomotion <Cite id="simdist-2026" />.

## Evaluation must use the same real anchor

Both simulator types can be wrong in correlated ways: a policy may exploit contact softness in physics or visual shortcuts in a world model. SIMPLER builds matched environments and correlates simulated with real policy performance <Cite id="simpler-2024" />. Apply that test to both types with several policy families and held-out environments, scored on the same real outcome ([world-model evaluation](/world-models/evaluation/)).

<Image id="isaac-lab-assembly-real-2025" />

<span id="a-selection-rule" />
## Choose by what can be specified and what the data cover

Use explicit physics when state and mechanics can be specified, counterfactuals are broad, constraints need inspection or parallel stepping matters most ([parallel simulation for RL](/rl-sim2real/parallel-sim-rl/)). Use a learned world model when real observations hold structure that is costly to author, data cover the decisions of interest and validation can anchor model error. Use a hybrid for a localized mismatch, as ANYmal's simulator did <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />; [classical control](/classical/control/) and [latent dynamics](/world-models/latent-dynamics/) cover the two ends.

## Multimodal demonstrations

When one operator passes an obstacle on the left and another on the right, mean-squared-error regression averages the demonstrations into a collision. Energy-based implicit policies often beat such explicit policies <Cite id="implicit-bc-2021" />, and diffusion models learn an expressive distribution over the joint action space <Cite id="pearce-diffusion-bc-2023" />. Pan et al. (2025) contest this motivation: generative policies owe their gains to supervised iterative computation, and a two-step regression policy essentially matches flow policies <Cite id="much-ado-noising-2025" />. Fine-tuned OpenVLA-OFT, an L1-regression VLA, beat from-scratch Diffusion Policy and ACT by up to 15 points of average success <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />.

## Denoising in action space

<DiffusionDenoising className="my-6" />

The policy is a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) <Cite id="ddpm-2020" /> conditioned on recent observations. Where a regression head computes $a_t = f_\theta(o_t)$, Diffusion Policy models $p(A_t \mid O_t)$ over the next $T_p$ actions. Inference starts from Gaussian noise and repeatedly subtracts a fraction of the noise that the denoiser $\epsilon_\theta$ predicts,

$$
A_t^{k-1} = \alpha \left( A_t^k - \gamma \, \epsilon_\theta(O_t, A_t^k, k) + \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I) \right)

## The contract has four parts

A contract names coordinates (joint, Cartesian, object-relative or another frame), semantics (absolute target, delta, velocity, force, torque or controller parameter), timing (rate, horizon and stale-prediction handling) and execution (interpolation, clipping, inverse kinematics, feedback and safety limits). DROID records equivalent commands in several action spaces <Cite id="droid-2024" />, and robosuite's controllers span joint and Cartesian spaces <Cite id="robosuite-2020" />.

## Joint-space actions

Joint position targets are a common imitation baseline; ACT predicts chunks of absolute joint-and-gripper targets for two ViperX arms <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. The controller interpolates and enforces limits, but one shoulder angle moves different arms differently.

Joint velocity targets drift when integrated; the [kinematics module](/classical/kinematics/) derives the forward map and Jacobian both need <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />. In locomotion RL, target joint angles with local feedback beat raw torques for learning speed, robustness and motion quality <Cite id="peng-action-space-2016" />.

## Cartesian actions

Cartesian actions say what the tool should do. Once range and frame are fixed, relative deltas from the current pose label arms with different joint counts and link lengths alike, provided each robot supplies inverse kinematics or an operational-space controller; Khatib's 1987 operational space formulation unifies motion and force control <Cite id="khatib-1987" />. Euler angles and quaternions are discontinuous as network outputs, while 6D representations are continuous <Cite id="rotation-continuity-2018" />.

GR00T N1.6's notes find relative actions smoother and more accurate than absolute ones but prone to error accumulation on small datasets <Cite id="gr00t-n1-6-2025" />, and in matched VLA pretraining ablations a unified end-effector-relative representation was critical for cross-embodiment transfer <Cite id="vla-scaling-alignment-2026" />. X-VLA instead learns a separate set of soft-prompt embeddings for each data source as embodiment-specific prompts <Cite id="x-vla-2025" />.

## Torque and impedance actions

Torque actions expose dynamics and contact; Levine et al. mapped raw images to motor torques <Cite id="levine-visuomotor-2015" />. They need a high rate and a safety layer that holds when the output is wrong: libfranka sends 1 kHz commands in five modes, including gravity- and friction-compensated joint torque <Cite id="franka-fci-docs" />, while Rudin et al.'s locomotion pipeline sends joint-position targets to a PD controller <Cite id="rudin-2021" />.

<Image id="adaptive-compliance-tasks-2024" />

Impedance actions sit between: the policy picks a pose target plus stiffness and damping, and a controller turns error into force. Hogan judged position or force control alone inadequate for manipulation <Cite id="hogan-1985" />. Task-space impedance references needed the fewest samples against torque, joint PD and inverse dynamics <Cite id="varin-action-spaces-2019" />, and Adaptive Compliance Policy's predicted compliance beats position-only visuomotor policies by over 50% <Cite id="acp-2024" />.

<ImpedancePress className="my-6" />

## Chunks change the time axis

An <Term id="action-chunking">action chunk</Term> predicts several steps per inference, which helped ACT and two retrofitted baselines ([action chunking](/manipulation/action-chunking/)) <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />; Diffusion Policy executes the first part of a predicted horizon, then replans <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />. Open-loop chunks go stale when contact changes the scene, which receding horizons, temporal ensembling and real-time chunk replacement each address <Cite id="real-time-chunking-2025" /> ([real-time execution](/manipulation/realtime-execution/)).

Rates differ by layer: GEN-1.5 produces 100 Hz action trajectories <Cite id="gen-1-5-2026" />, and Helix 02's S0 sends joint-level actuator commands at 1 kHz beneath S1's 200 Hz joint targets <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />. Report predicted and executed horizons separately.

## Tokens change the output geometry

RT-2 <Cite id="rt2-2023" /> and OpenVLA map continuous actions to vocabulary tokens to reuse language-model training, OpenVLA binning seven dimensions into 256 values <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. Binning allows cross-entropy but limits resolution and adds autoregressive decoding to latency. BEAST encodes sequences as fixed-length B-spline tokens, allowing parallel decoding without separate tokenizer training <Cite id="beast-2025" />.

FAST compresses a chunk's frequency coefficients with byte-pair encoding, far better than per-dimension binning, and its universal FAST+ tokenizer was trained on 1M real robot action trajectories <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />. ActionCodec evaluates tokenizers by optimization properties, including temporal overlap, vocabulary redundancy and token independence <Cite id="actioncodec-2026" />. VQ-BeT's vector-quantized actions infer 5 times faster than Diffusion Policy <Cite id="vq-bet-2024" />, and LAP writes end-effector motions as short natural-language phrases, with LAP-3B averaging over 50% zero-shot success on three unseen robots <Cite id="lap-2026" />.

Continuous heads skip tokens: OpenVLA-OFT's continuous actions, parallel decoding and L1 objective lifted LIBERO success from 76.5% to 97.1% <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />, and Figure says Helix outputs continuous control to avoid tokenization <Cite id="helix-2025" />. Naively adding a continuous expert to a VLM harms training speed and knowledge transfer, which [knowledge insulation](/manipulation/knowledge-insulation/) addresses <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

Zeji Yi, Max Simchowitz, Guanya Shi and colleagues at Carnegie Mellon and Amazon FAR (October 2026) gave one PaliGemma VLA four action heads: continuous or binned into 512 values, each predicted in one pass or by iterative flow. On simulated RoboCasa, over five seeds of 500 episodes, binned flow reached 53.9% success, continuous flow 52.7% and one-pass continuous regression 38.8%. One-pass binned prediction reached 27.1%, which the authors trace to tokens chosen independently across time steps and action dimensions; guidance raised it to 49.2% <Cite id="discrete-actions-2026" />.

## A selection rule

Choose the lowest-level action the task requires and the platform supports safely. Across 13,000+ real rollouts and 500+ models, predicting delta actions consistently helped, with joint space favoring control stability and task space favoring generalization <Cite id="action-space-design-2026" />. Hold controller, rate, horizon and observation history fixed when comparing architectures, or the comparison measures interface changes. In one vision-based sim-to-real study of picking and pushing, joint velocity beat the tested pose and joint-increment alternatives <Cite id="rl-action-spaces-2026" />.

<ActionSpaceTable className="my-6" />

## Domain randomization: train on a distribution of simulators

Jakobi and colleagues found in 1995 that sim-to-real correspondence depended on how much noise the simulation used <Cite id="jakobi-1995" />. Tobin and colleagues randomized textures, lighting and camera pose for tabletop object localization; their best network localized objects to about 1.5 cm over 480 webcam images of eight geometric objects, though most runs used ImageNet initialization (random initialization nearly matched it given enough simulated data), and their abstract frames the real world as "just another variation" once the simulator varies enough <Cite id="tobin-2017" />.

Peng and colleagues randomized link mass, joint damping, friction, controller gains, action timing and observation noise, maximizing expected return over [that dynamics distribution](/how-robots-work/#worlds). A recurrent policy trained only in simulation pushed a puck with a seven-DoF Fetch arm, with start and target positions randomized within a 30 cm square <Cite id="peng-2018" />. Chen and colleagues' analysis bounds the sim-to-real gap and highlights the importance of history-dependent policies <Cite id="chen-dr-theory-2021" />.

<Image id="mujoco-playground-franka-block-2025" />

OpenAI's 2018 hand policy randomized friction coefficients and object appearance and transferred to the physical robot <Cite id="openai-dactyl-2018" />. Its Rubik's-cube successor added a <Term id="curriculum-learning">curriculum</Term> version, automatic domain randomization, which widens ranges as the policy succeeds <Cite id="openai-rubiks-cube-2019" />.

Isaac Lab, the [GPU-parallel training framework](/rl-sim2real/parallel-sim-rl), ships ADR as a configurable curriculum, but mass, friction, contact offsets and joint armature change through PhysX CPU APIs. Most parameters randomize at runtime, mesh scale and collider type only before simulation starts <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />. SPI-Active notes that poorly tuned randomization "can lead to overly conservative policies" <Cite id="spi-active-2025" />.

## Teacher-student distillation: privilege in, proprioception out

Teacher-student training splits sensing from control: a teacher learns from privileged simulator state, then a student with deployable sensing imitates it. Learning by Cheating used this two-stage form for driving <Cite id="learning-by-cheating-2019" />, after asymmetric actor-critic had given only the critic full state <Cite id="asymmetric-ac-2017" />.

Lee and colleagues distilled a privileged RL teacher, which saw simulator-only terrain and contact information, into a temporal convolutional student via its actions and latent features. The student uses two seconds of <Term id="proprioception">proprioceptive</Term> history, plus the command and current state, and one controller per robot generation took ANYmal-B and ANYmal-C robots through mud, snow, rubble and vegetation without environment-specific tuning <Cite id="lee-2020" />. Isaac Lab's DextrAH-RGB example distills a privileged KUKA and Allegro teacher into a stereo-RGB network <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />, and VIRAL's authors report that scaling to tens of GPUs, up to 64, made teacher and student training reliable for an RGB humanoid that ran up to 54 loco-manipulation cycles <Cite id="viral-2025" />.

RMA trains a base policy and an environment-factor encoder jointly with RL, then regresses an adaptation module on simulated state-action histories to predict the latent extrinsics. The module reads 50 state-action steps (0.5 seconds) and updates asynchronously at about 10 Hz on the A1, while the base policy runs at 100 Hz on the latest estimate, with no online gradient updates. The paper reports adaptation in fractions of a second without real-world fine-tuning, and failures after large perturbations or multiple leg obstructions; its latent encodes behavior-relevant conditions without guaranteeing each physical parameter <Cite id="rma-2021" />. UP-OSI had earlier fed dynamics parameters predicted from recent history into a universal policy <Cite id="up-osi-2017" />.

Isaac Lab calls the failure mode an information gap due to input mismatch: the student must reconstruct unobserved states from partial observations such as images, hardest under heavy camera occlusion <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />. The teacher-student panel illustrates this with authored terrain and noise, so its errors rise by construction.

<TeacherStudent className="my-6" />

Tan and colleagues paired an identified actuator model and simulated latency with randomization <Cite id="tan-quadruped-2018" />. SPI-Active samples parameters in parallel with Fisher-information-driven excitation and beats baselines by 42 to 63% in locomotion tasks <Cite id="spi-active-2025" />, and Miller and colleagues tune Spot simulation against hardware with CMA-ES <Cite id="miller-spot-2025" />. An Unsupervised Actuator Net fits complex actuation from real data without torque sensing, supporting athletic loco-manipulation transfer <Cite id="fey-athletic-2025" />.

ASAP pretrains phase-conditioned tracking policies in IsaacGym on <Term id="retargeting">retargeted</Term> human motions, runs them on a Unitree G1, and records trajectories with motion capture and onboard sensors. A second PPO policy learns a delta action added before the simulator step, the tracking policy is fine-tuned with the frozen delta model in simulation, and only the tracking policy is deployed. For the hardware study the delta covers only four ankle DoFs of the 23-DoF model <Cite id="asap-2025" />. HALO calibrates the unloaded robot first, then identifies an unknown payload's mass distribution with differentiable simulation <Cite id="halo-payload-2026" />.

Evaluation separates IsaacGym-to-IsaacSim and IsaacGym-to-Genesis tests, with open-loop replay and closed-loop tracking over 43 motion sequences, and ASAP does not win every metric: in the easy IsaacSim closed-loop group its mean global joint-position error is 106 mm against SysID's 105 mm. On hardware, compared only with Vanilla, the error falls from 61.2 to 50.2 mm on kicking and from 159 to 112 mm on LeBron James's "Silencer" <Cite id="asap-2025" />. ASAP reports better tracking on the held-out "Silencer" motion without establishing coverage of arbitrary unseen skills, and its stated hardware limits are motor overheating and damage, motion-capture dependence and the data needed for a full 23-DoF delta model <Cite id="asap-2025" />. Swift's champion-level drone racing likewise combined simulation RL with physical-world data <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />.

## Real-to-sim: rebuild the scene, keep the physics

edits.before:
RoboGSim's August 2025 revision chains a Gaussian Reconstructor, Digital Twins Builder, Scene Composer and Interactive Engine, where mesh assets and measured layout connect it to Isaac Sim. Novel-pose rendering and trajectory replay are evaluated separately. Closed-loop policies act on splat renders while Isaac Sim handles kinematics and collisions. On UR5 ring-toss, ten trials with up to three grasps each, the real-data model placed 90% on the real robot but 30% in RoboGSim, so its scores cannot replace real-robot tests <Cite id="robogsim-2024" />.

Newer twins go beyond static appearance: RialTo runs RL in digital twins built from small amounts of real data, raising imitation-policy robustness by over 67% <Cite id="rialto-2024" />, and PolaRiS turns short video scans into environments that track real generalist-policy performance better than existing benchmarks <Cite id="polaris-2025" />. SimFoundry's simulated evaluations correlated with real results at a mean Pearson coefficient of 0.911 across 7 tasks and 5 policy architectures <Cite id="simfoundry-2026" />, and NVIDIA's Newton 1.0 post describes a tiled camera sensor that ray-traces both triangle meshes and Gaussian splats <Cite id="newton-manipulation-blog-2026" />.

A rebuilt twin can still mislead. Kadian and colleagues measured a sim-versus-real success correlation of 0.18 in a 3D-scanned lab because agents exploited collision dynamics, and tuning simulation parameters raised it to 0.844 <Cite id="kadian-2019" />.

Kaiyuan Chen, Ken Goldberg and colleagues at UC Berkeley and NVIDIA (October 2026) built RoboSimStudio, which lets people and coding agents edit the solver, contact model and physical parameters of a Newton simulation <Cite id="robosimstudio-2026" />. In a pilot, coding agents built a bimanual sponge-wiping simulation from a smartphone video in about an hour, and a policy improved there completed the wipe on the real robot <Cite id="robosimstudio-2026" />. One real rollout then displaced a bar support that the simulation held fixed, and the authors judged sim and real agreement on this single task mainly by qualitative observation <Cite id="robosimstudio-2026" />.

## Levers behind successful transfer

<CollaborativeOperationModes className="my-6" />

Marvel and Norcross summarise the four scenarios from ISO/TS 15066 (2016). Two are procedural: a safety-rated monitored stop permits no motion while a person is present, and hand guiding gives the operator the control channel. Two are quantitative: <Term id="speed-and-separation-monitoring">speed and separation monitoring</Term> keeps a computed distance between robot and person, while <Term id="power-and-force-limiting">power and force limiting</Term> gives up distance and bounds the contact <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

ISO/TS 15066, published in 2016, supplemented the 2011 ISO 10218 for collaborative operation and is now marked for revision <Cite id="iso-ts-15066" />. The 2025 revision of ISO 10218 integrated it normatively and introduced new classifications for collaborative applications, Hartmann and colleagues report <Cite id="hartmann-iso-10218-2026" />.

## Separation criteria assume a person approaching at 1600 to 2000 mm/s

Marvel and Norcross reproduce the ISO 13855:2010 decision criteria: an intrusion margin of at least 850 mm for a normal approach protected by multiple separate beams, against 1200 mm for a single-height beam. A two-handed control device may reduce the margin to 250 mm, but they exclude typical two-handed teach pendants from that exception and doubt that stationary-machinery criteria transfer to robots <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

For operator approach they call 1600 mm/s a worst-case assumption and report a 2000 mm/s stationary-machinery maximum, with the 1600 mm/s option only when separation is greater than 500 mm. Approach speed may be measured directly; otherwise it is typically assumed constant and directed toward the robot. They add that 2000 mm/s may be more prudent for rapid motions and detection uncertainty, and a risk assessment may call for a faster approach <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

The instrument is an authored teaching model whose defaults are not certified limits: C = 0.85 m, 10 m/s² deceleration, a 0.1 s reaction delay, 0.1 m position uncertainty and a 1.6 m workcell. A 100 Hz update period is 0.01 s, which says nothing about detect-to-command latency. The NIST paper calls its early-draft equation a rough approximation and requires traceable stopping-time and braking-distance measurements for a real robot <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

## Force limits rest on measured pain thresholds by body region

Haddadin, Albu-Schäffer and Hirzinger made the force question empirical with crash-test impacts <Cite id="haddadin-2009" />. Later pain-threshold studies, such as Han and colleagues' 37-subject impactor tests, report limits by body region and contact geometry <Cite id="han-force-pain-2024" />. A power-and-force-limited application therefore attaches a measured number to a named body part, the value the [contact-force lab in the control module](/classical/control/) also reads <Cite id="han-force-pain-2024" />.

<span id="the-stack-the-standards-actually-form" />
## Risk assessment comes first, and a compliant robot does not make a compliant cell

<Term id="risk-assessment">Risk assessment</Term> begins with ISO 12100, the general-principles standard for machinery safety, at edition 1 since 2010 and due to be replaced by a revision now in draft <Cite id="iso-12100" />. Its abstract describes the procedure: identify the hazards, estimate and evaluate the risks, then reduce them, documenting and verifying each step <Cite id="iso-12100" />. The reduction measures form a hierarchy: design the hazard out, guard against what remains, then inform the operator, the "3-step approach" OSHA's manual reproduces from the robot industry association <Cite id="osha-otm-robots" />.

The robot-specific layer splits liability in two. ISO 10218-1 covers the robot as partly completed machinery, the manufacturer's obligation; ISO 10218-2 covers the application and its cell, the integrator's <Cite id="iso-10218-1-2025" /> <Cite id="iso-10218-2-2025" />. Both were republished in February 2025 at editions 3 and 2, the first major revision since 2011. The US adoption, ANSI/A3 R15.06-2025, added a Part 3, approved on October 7, 2025, that gives guidance to users of industrial robot cells <Cite id="a3-r1506-2025-store" /> <Cite id="rr-ansi-r1506-2026" />.

## Safety controls carry rated integrity levels, and an emergency stop cannot detect a hazard

<Term id="functional-safety">Functional safety</Term> grades the control system that enforces these requirements. IEC 61508, whose Part 1 is at edition 2 from 2010, is the generic standard for electrical, electronic and programmable systems that carry out safety functions, rated by <Term id="safety-integrity-level">safety integrity level</Term> <Cite id="iec-61508-1-2010" />. ISO 13849-1, at edition 4 from 2023, is the machinery counterpart for safety-related control parts, including software, rated by <Term id="performance-level">performance level</Term>; it defers low-demand operation to IEC 61508 <Cite id="iso-13849-1-2023" />.

ISO 13850, at edition 3 from 2015, specifies the <Term id="emergency-stop">emergency stop</Term> independently of the energy source and names IEC 60204-1, at its 2016 edition, for the electrical realisation <Cite id="iso-13850-2015" /> <Cite id="iec-60204-1-2016" />. The button cannot detect a hazard; it waits for a person to see one and press. In stop category 0 the actuators lose power and the brakes engage, while in category 1 power is maintained through a controlled stop <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

<Image id="emergency-stop-siemens-2006" />

For mobile robots, ISO 3691-4, at edition 2 from 2023, covers driverless industrial trucks, naming automated guided vehicles and autonomous mobile robots among its examples <Cite id="iso-3691-4-2023" />. In the United States the R15.08 series covers industrial mobile robots, with Part 1 published in 2020 and Part 2 in 2023 <Cite id="a3-robot-safety-standards" />.

<span id="the-humanoid-gap-and-the-standard-that-is-not-finished" />
### The humanoid standard is still a committee draft at stage 30.60

A humanoid falls, a hazard class the industrial documents were not written for. ISO/CD 25785-1 covers industrial mobile robots that need active control to remain balanced, including bipedal machines <Cite id="iso-cd-25785-1" />. It is a committee draft: the comment period closed on 8 July 2026, and in late October 2026 the catalogue still showed stage 30.60, with edition 1 unpublished and no date for the next stage <Cite id="iso-cd-25785-1" />. A parallel technical report for the United States and Canada, ANSI/A3 TR R15.108, is under development for dynamically stable industrial mobile robots including humanoids <Cite id="agility-digit-5-2026" />.

Until those documents are agreed, a humanoid deployed beside people runs under a risk assessment that invents its own treatment of fall risk. Agility reports that Digit 5 avoids people, stops or sits down under an independent safety controller, and that Digit passed an independent field evaluation on a customer production line against safety standards administered by OSHA <Cite id="agility-digit-5-2026" />. Brooks predicts that without new types of mechanical systems walking humanoids "will remain too unsafe to be in close proximity to real humans" <Cite id="brooks-scorecard-2026" />.

OSHA's technical manual chapter on industrial robots covers safeguarding devices, the teach-pendant hazard and lockout and tagout, with accident descriptions <Cite id="osha-otm-robots" />. NIOSH counted 41 robot-related workplace fatalities in the United States from 1992 to 2017. Most involved stationary robots (83%) striking the worker under their own power (78%), often during maintenance <Cite id="layne-robot-fatalities-2023" />.

<span id="why-a-learned-policy-cannot-be-certified" />
## Certification needs a specification beyond the policy weights

A safety integrity level and a performance level are both assigned to a safety function <Cite id="iso-13849-1-2023" />. Both presume a verifiable specification of what the function must do, and a development process that avoids systematic faults, the design errors that redundant hardware cannot remove.

Policy weights alone do not state which behaviours must be excluded or document how systematic faults were prevented. Luckcuck and colleagues find testing and simulation insufficient evidence for certifying autonomous robots <Cite id="luckcuck-formal-2019" />. Kalra and Paddock calculate that existing fleets would need tens and sometimes hundreds of years of driving to demonstrate autonomous-vehicle reliability <Cite id="kalra-paddock-2016" />, and [deployment numbers](/frontier/reliability-gap/) show the same distance.

Properties of a neural network can be checked in restricted settings. Reluplex extends the simplex method to ReLU activations and demonstrated property verification on prototype ACAS Xu aircraft collision-avoidance networks <Cite id="reluplex-2017" />.

<span id="the-pattern-a-verifiable-layer-wrapping-an-unverifiable-one" />
### A verifiable safety filter can wrap an unverifiable policy

What ships instead puts something simple enough to verify between the black-box policy and the actuators, with authority to override. ISO/IEC TR 5469 (2024) names this use: non-AI safety related functions that ensure safety for AI-controlled equipment <Cite id="iso-iec-tr-5469-2024" />.

The formal instance is the safety filter. A <Term id="control-barrier-function">control barrier function</Term> defines a set the system must stay inside and turns forward invariance of that set into a constraint on the commanded input, enforced each step <Cite id="ames-cbf-2019" />. Wabersich and colleagues survey the family, including reachability and predictive variants, and describe a filter that takes a proposed input from any source and modifies it as little as necessary <Cite id="wabersich-safety-filters-2023" />.

The mechanism varies with the specification. Ames and colleagues combine barrier constraints with Lyapunov performance objectives in a quadratic program <Cite id="cbf-qp-2016" />. A predictive filter instead checks a proposed input through model predictive control with state- and input-dependent uncertainty <Cite id="predictive-safety-filter-2018" />. A temporal-logic shield can restrict the available actions or correct one that violates its specification <Cite id="shielding-2017" />.

Runtime assurance can also switch controllers. Neural Simplex transfers control to a baseline when the neural controller proposes a potentially unsafe input, and adds retraining and a route back to the advanced controller <Cite id="neural-simplex-2019" />.

Learning a barrier still needs assumptions. Robey and colleagues learn one from safe expert trajectories for a known control-affine dynamical system, with guarantees under specified smoothness conditions <Cite id="learn-cbf-2020" />. CPO instead targets near-constraint satisfaction during policy optimization and tests safety-motivated constraints in simulated locomotion <Cite id="constrained-policy-2017" />.

<SafetyFilterFence className="my-6" />

In 2026 the pattern reached vision-language-action policies. VLPSA wraps π0.5 in a full-body CBF-QP safety filter without retraining, and on SafeLIBERO it raised collision avoidance from 23.1% to 91.2% while surpassing the base policy's task success <Cite id="vlpsa-2026" />.

### Barrier functions now reach slender robots, and industrial limiters remain the norm

Barrier functions are also being adapted to bodies that rigid-arm controllers handle poorly. In September 2026, Zijian Cai, Daniela Rus, Cecilia Laschi and colleagues weighted the control barrier functions along a slender hyper-redundant robot to enforce obstacle constraints while correcting tracking errors from uneven loading. On a circular path-following task with obstacles, fixed weights cut the root-mean-square tracking error of the unweighted method by up to 59.6% in simulation and 87.7% in physical experiments <Cite id="wcbf-hyper-redundant-2026" />.

<Image id="wcbf-hyper-redundant-robot-2026" />

The industrial instance is cruder and far more widely deployed: force limiting in the actuator, velocity limiting in the drive, and workspace limiting in the safety controller. The standards above know how to rate those mechanisms, whatever generated the trajectory. Guardrails inside a model are no substitute: RoboPAIR jailbroke LLM-controlled robots, often with 100% attack success, including a deployed Unitree Go2 <Cite id="robopair-2024" />.

<span id="the-assurance-case-for-what-testing-cannot-reach" />
### A safety case argues for what testing cannot show

What the wrapper leaves over gets a <Term id="safety-case">safety case</Term>: a structured, documented argument that a system is acceptably safe in a stated environment, with evidence attached to each step. UL 4600, at edition 3 from March 2023, applies the approach to autonomous products <Cite id="ul-4600-2023" />. The Goal Structuring Notation community standard, version 3, supplies the usual notation, decomposing a top-level goal into subgoals that each rest on cited evidence <Cite id="gsn-standard-v3" />. For ML components, AMLAS supplies safety case patterns and a process for generating the evidence base <Cite id="amlas-2021" />.

An argument built to conclude that a system is safe will usually reach that conclusion, and Koopman argues that "safe enough" means more than crashes divided by miles <Cite id="koopman-safe-enough-2026" />. The alternative is a rule set formal enough to check, which Shalev-Shwartz, Shammah and Shashua proposed as responsibility-sensitive safety <Cite id="rss-2017" />. Robotics is inheriting that decade-long [autonomous vehicles](/adjacent/autonomous-vehicles/) argument late.

<span id="the-machine-learning-half-of-the-wrapper" />
## Conformal prediction and monitors tell a learned system when to stop or ask

<Term id="conformal-prediction">Conformal prediction</Term> turns any model's raw output into a prediction set with a guaranteed coverage rate under exchangeability. Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer built the framework <Cite id="vovk-conformal-2022" />, and Angelopoulos and Bates's tutorial carried it into general machine-learning practice <Cite id="angelopoulos-conformal-2021" />. The 2025 revision of ISO 10218 integrated it normatively and introduced classifications for collaborative applications, Hartmann and colleagues report <Cite id="hartmann-iso-10218-2026" />.

Marvel and Norcross reproduce the ISO 13855:2010 decision criteria: an intrusion margin of at least 850 mm for normal approach protected by multiple separate beams, against 1200 mm for a single-height beam. A two-handed control device may reduce the margin to 250 mm, but they exclude typical two-handed teach pendants from that exception and doubt stationary-machinery criteria transfer to robots <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

For operator approach they call 1600 mm/s a worst-case assumption and report a 2000 mm/s stationary-machinery maximum, with the 1600 mm/s option only when separation is greater than 500 mm. Approach speed may be measured directly; otherwise it is typically assumed constant and directed toward the robot. They add 2000 mm/s may be more prudent for rapid motions and detection uncertainty, and risk assessment may require a faster approach <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

The instrument is an authored teaching model whose defaults are not certified limits: C = 0.85 m, 10 m/s² deceleration, a 0.1 s reaction delay, 0.1 m position uncertainty and a 1.6 m workcell. A 100 Hz update period is 0.01 s, revealing nothing about detect-to-command latency. The NIST paper calls its early-draft equation a rough approximation and requires traceable stopping-time and braking-distance measurements for real robots <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

Haddadin, Albu-Schäffer and Hirzinger made the force question empirical with crash-test impacts <Cite id="haddadin-2009" />. Later pain-threshold studies, including Han and colleagues' 37-subject impactor tests, report limits by body region and contact geometry <Cite id="han-force-pain-2024" />. A power-and-force-limited application therefore attaches a measured number to a named body part, the value the [contact-force lab in the control module](/classical/control/) also reads <Cite id="han-force-pain-2024" />.

## Risk assessment comes first, and a compliant robot does not make a compliant cell

<Term id="risk-assessment">Risk assessment</Term> begins with ISO 12100, the general-principles standard for machinery safety, at edition 1 since 2010 and awaiting replacement by a draft revision <Cite id="iso-12100" />. Its abstract specifies: identify hazards, estimate and evaluate risks, then reduce them, documenting and verifying each step <Cite id="iso-12100" />. Risk reduction follows a hierarchy: design the hazard out, guard against what remains, then inform the operator, the "3-step approach" OSHA's manual reproduces from the robot industry association <Cite id="osha-otm-robots" />.

Robot-specific standards split liability in two. ISO 10218-1 covers the robot as partly completed machinery, the manufacturer's obligation; ISO 10218-2 covers the application and its cell, the integrator's <Cite id="iso-10218-1-2025" /> <Cite id="iso-10218-2-2025" />. Both were republished February 2025 at editions 3 and 2, the first major revision since 2011. The US adoption, ANSI/A3 R15.06-2025, added Part 3, approved October 7, 2025, guiding industrial robot cell users <Cite id="a3-r1506-2025-store" /> <Cite id="rr-ansi-r1506-2026" />.

<Term id="functional-safety">Functional safety</Term> grades the control system enforcing these requirements. IEC 61508, with Part 1 at edition 2 from 2010, is the generic standard for electrical, electronic and programmable systems performing safety functions, rated by <Term id="safety-integrity-level">safety integrity level</Term> <Cite id="iec-61508-1-2010" />. Safety integrity levels and performance levels are assigned to safety functions <Cite id="iso-13849-1-2023" />. Both presume a verifiable specification of the function's requirements, and a development process avoiding systematic faults, design errors redundant hardware cannot remove.

Policy weights alone do not state which behaviours must be excluded or document how systematic faults were prevented. Luckcuck and colleagues find testing and simulation insufficient evidence for certifying autonomous robots <Cite id="luckcuck-formal-2019" />. <span id="the-pattern-a-verifiable-layer-wrapping-an-unverifiable-one" />

Shipped systems put a simple, verifiable mechanism between the black-box policy and actuators, with override authority. ISO/IEC TR 5469 (2024) names this use: non-AI safety related functions that ensure safety for AI-controlled equipment <Cite id="iso-iec-tr-5469-2024" />.

<span id="what-would-actually-close-this" />
## Three missing pieces block certification of learned systems

The first missing piece is a specification language in which a manipulation task's safety requirement can be written precisely enough to check <Cite id="luckcuck-formal-2019" />. The second is a humanoid standard past committee draft, giving fall risk an agreed treatment <Cite id="iso-cd-25785-1" />. The third is a published assurance case for a deployed learned system, complete enough that an outsider could dispute a specific step <Cite id="amlas-2021" />.

A position paper from October 2026, by researchers at Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna, MIT CSAIL and four other universities, asks for the same kind of evidence on the human side of the interaction. Niccolò Pagliarani, Maximilian Stölzle, Daniela Rus, Matteo Cianchetti and colleagues argue that a claim that a robot is trustworthy around people should rest on evidence for three properties in the intended setting: bounded physical risk, behavior that people can anticipate, and expectations that match what the robot has shown it can and cannot do. In their view these should guide design and evaluation from the outset, and the paper offers candidate evaluation criteria as a research agenda, with no new measurements <Cite id="trustworthy-physical-ai-2026" />.

Try Preorder, Humanoids and \$1k-\$10k together and one row remains: Noetix's Bumi, announced for presale in October 2025 at ¥9,998, about \$1,400 <Cite id="noetix-bumi-2025" /> <Cite id="bjnews-noetix-bumi-2025" />.

Noetix lists Bumi at 98 cm tall and 17 kg, with 21 total degrees of freedom <Cite id="noetix-bumi-page-2026" />.

## Arms, from \$122 to \$70,000

The SO-101 is a 3D-printed arm with six <Term id="degrees-of-freedom">degrees of freedom</Term>, five joints plus a gripper, built from STS3215 servos. Its community BOM for one follower arm totals \$121.94 in the US column <Cite id="so-arm100-repo-2026" />. Seeed Studio sells the SO-ARM101 Pro at \$295 unassembled or \$299 assembled, with 12-bit magnetic encoders and a 500 g payload <Cite id="seeed-so-arm101-pro-2026" />. LeRobot runs ACT, π0 and SmolVLA policies on these arms <Cite id="lerobot-docs-2026" />. Pull the arm apart in the figure below, then guess which motor works hardest to hold it out straight.

<ExplainerFigure id="arm" />

Trossen Robotics renamed its ALOHA line Trossen AI. Its Solo AI, Stationary AI and Mobile AI kits list at \$11,385.95, \$23,995.95 and \$33,695.95 and integrate LeRobot and OpenPI <Cite id="trossen-ai-2026" />. The WidowX AI arm, sold in leader and follower forms for <Term id="teleoperation">teleoperation</Term>, lists at \$4,545.95 in its base configuration, with six DoF, a 1.5 kg payload and 700 mm reach <Cite id="trossen-widowx-ai-2026" />.

ALOHA 2 succeeds the bimanual ALOHA rig behind ACT <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" /> and Mobile ALOHA <Cite id="mobile-aloha-2024" />; its hardware designs are open source, and the paper gives no price <Cite id="aloha-2-2024" />. Hugging Face, which bought Pollen Robotics in April 2025, sells the Reachy 2 humanoid for \$70,000 <Cite id="hf-pollen-acquisition-2025" />. The seven-DoF Franka Emika Panda collected DROID's 76,000 trajectories <Cite id="droid-2024" />.

<Image id="franka-emika-panda-cebit-2017" />

## Humanoids: shipping beat shouting

Omdia counts about 13,000 [humanoids shipped](/market-map) in 2025, including 5,168 from AgiBot, 39 percent of the total <Cite id="agibot-omdia-ranking-2026" />, a figure that also counts its mobile manipulators <Cite id="agibot-omdia-2026" />. IFR counts about 7,000 full-size humanoids (above 140 cm) sold in 2025, often in applications still requiring human teleoperation <Cite id="ifr-service-robots-2026" />. Unitree's May 2026 IPO prospectus reports over 5,500 humanoids shipped in 2025, excluding wheeled dual-arm robots, and calls that the world's highest total <Cite id="unitree-prospectus-2026" />.

Unitree's R1 AIR lists at \$4,900 with 20 DoF and the R1 at \$5,900 with 26 <Cite id="unitree-r1-2026" />. The G1 lists at \$13,500 for the base model with 23 DoF, and its EDU configuration spans 23 to 43 DoF by quote <Cite id="unitree-g1-2026" />. The H2 has [31 DoF](/how-robots-work/#humanoid) (six per leg, seven per arm, three waist, two head), 360 N·m of joint torque and a 2,070 TOPS onboard chip <Cite id="unitree-h2-2026" />.

Configuration matters when comparing joint counts. Fourier lists up to 55 actuators for GR-3 with its optional 12-DoF hands <Cite id="fourier-gr3-docs-2026" />. LimX lists 31 active DoF for Oli and lists its end-effector options separately <Cite id="limx-oli-spec-2026" />.

1X sells the NEO for \$20,000 or \$499 a month after a refundable \$200 deposit, with US deliveries starting in 2026 <Cite id="1x-order-2026" />. In April 2026 it reported capacity for 10,000 NEOs a year and said some buyers would get theirs that year, others later <Cite id="1x-neo-factory-2026" />.

Boston Dynamics' electric Atlas has 56 DoF with continuous rotation at key joints, a 50 kg instant payload, IP67 sealing and a 4-hour swappable battery <Cite id="bd-atlas-2026" />, and it reaches 2.3 m <Cite id="bd-atlas-unveil-2026" />. Hyundai Motor Group plans 25,000 Atlas units for its plants over the next few years, plus a US factory able to build 30,000 robots a year <Cite id="bd-rmac-2026" />.

Figure's third-generation humanoid has a palm camera in each hand, no disclosed hand DoF and 2 kW wireless charging through its feet. Figure builds it for high-volume manufacturing at its BotQ facility <Cite id="figure-03-2025" />, whose first line can make up to 12,000 humanoids a year <Cite id="figure-botq-2025" />. Agility says Digit 5, unveiled in September 2026, repeatedly lifts loads up to 22.7 kg and runs 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, with general availability by the end of 2027 <Cite id="agility-digit-5-2026" />. Tesla says it is installing the first Optimus production lines at Fremont and will use the first builds to collect training data <Cite id="tesla-q2-2026-update" />.

<Image id="atlas-darpa-frontview-2013" />

## Hands, bundled and standalone

<span id="hands-ship-bundled" />Most [dexterous hands](/frontier/dexterity) ship with a robot: Unitree's Dex3-1, a G1 EDU option, has seven active DoF per hand (three thumb, two index, two middle) and an optional tactile array <Cite id="unitree-g1-2026" />. 1X's order page lists 22 DoF per NEO hand <Cite id="1x-neo-2026" />. Its July 9, 2026 hand post counts 25, adding 3 wrist DoF to the 22 fully actuated ones in the fingers and palm <Cite id="1x-neos-hands-2026" />. Boston Dynamics' October 2026 Atlas hand has four fingers and 13 DoF, with pressure sensors over the fingertips and palm <Cite id="bd-atlas-hand-2026" />.

The open LEAP Hand has 16 DoF and costs about \$2,000 in catalog parts, roughly an eighth of the Allegro Hand it was benchmarked against <Cite id="leap-hand-2023" />. RUKA's authors put the Allegro at \$15,000 and built a five-fingered hand for under \$1,300 <Cite id="ruka-2025" />. ORCA is an open 17-DoF tendon-driven hand with tactile sensors, under 2,000 CHF in materials <Cite id="orca-hand-2025" />, and the commercial Shadow Dexterous Hand uses 20 motors for 24 degrees of freedom <Cite id="shadow-dexterous-hand-2026" />. Sharpa's Wave, a human-scale five-finger hand with 22 active DoF and high-resolution tactile sensing, is sold through a sales enquiry and lists no price <Cite id="sharpa-wave-2026" />. PSYONIC designed its Ability Hand as a prosthesis and opened it to robotics researchers in November 2022 <Cite id="psyonic-ability-hand-2022" />.

Unitree lists its standalone Dex5-1 at 20 total DoF, 16 of them active, with 94 tactile sensors per hand <Cite id="unitree-dex5-1-2026" />.

## Sensors: touch is the missing channel

Generalist policies mostly train on vision and <Term id="proprioception">proprioception</Term>, and DROID's Franka rig has three cameras and no touch sensing <Cite id="droid-2024" />. AgiBot World's humanoids add visuo-tactile sensors to the camera rig <Cite id="agibot-world-2025" />. A 2025 outlook in IEEE Transactions on Robotics blames divergent transduction methods with no standardized evaluation, poor durability, hysteresis and temperature sensitivity <Cite id="tactile-outlook-2025" />.

Perception hardware extends beyond ordinary cameras: ENGINEAI describes the SE01 sensor stack as lidar, depth cameras and infrared cameras <Cite id="engineai-se01-2026" />.

Chris Paxton of Agility Robotics argued on October 12, after IROS 2026, that multi-fingered hands may need the touch sensing two-finger grippers can do without, because their fingers increasingly hide the contacts a camera would need to see. He called tendon-driven hands now sold off the shelf a significant step toward making human-like dexterity "an intelligence problem, instead of a hardware design problem" <Cite id="paxton-iros-2026" />.

The GelSight Mini retails at \$500 and Meta FAIR's open DIGIT fingertip at \$350 <Cite id="tactile-outlook-2025" /> <Cite id="digit-sensor-2020" />. DIGIT's successor, Digit 360, has about 8.3 million taxels and resolves normal and shear forces to 1.01 mN and 1.27 mN <Cite id="digit-360-2024" />. GelSight manufactures it under a partnership Meta announced in October 2024 <Cite id="meta-fair-touch-2024" />. AnySkin, a magnetic skin, is the first uncalibrated tactile sensor reported to carry learned policies across replacement skins <Cite id="anyskin-2024" />.

Optical designs differ in the contacts they can observe. GelSlim 3.0 measures shape, contact-force distributions and incipient slip in a compact finger <Cite id="gelslim3-2021" />. GelTip views a deformable finger from its base, capturing contacts inside and outside the gripper closure <Cite id="geltip-2021" />. DenseTact estimates 3D surface deformation from fisheye camera images <Cite id="densetact-2022" />; AllSight estimates contact position, forces and torsion on a rounded finger <Cite id="allsight-2023" />.

## Compute: closing the loop

NVIDIA's Jetson Thor T5000 delivers 2,070 sparse FP4 TFLOPS with 128 GB of LPDDR5X at 273 GB/s on a 14-core Neoverse-V3AE CPU, within 40-130 W. The T4000 has 1,200 TFLOPS and 64 GB <Cite id="jetson-thor-2026" />. NVIDIA rates Thor at 7.5x the AI compute of Jetson Orin and launched the developer kit at \$3,499 in August 2025 <Cite id="nvidia-jetson-thor-available-2025" />. It now lists the kit at \$5,499, and the T5000 and T4000 modules at \$4,999 and \$2,999 in 1,000-unit volume <Cite id="nvidia-jetson-faq" />.

The 1X NEO runs on a Jetson Thor at up to 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS <Cite id="1x-neo-2026" />. Figure's Helix runs entirely on embedded low-power GPUs, with a 7-9 Hz vision-language model guiding a 200 Hz controller <Cite id="helix-2025" />.

VLA-Perf's roofline model predicts π0 inference at 19.0 Hz on Jetson Thor, 32.2 Hz on RTX 4090, 61.7 Hz on A100, 162.5 Hz on H100 and 314.4 Hz on B100, without network latency. These are batch-one analytical predictions for the 2.7B π0 baseline, with 3 cameras, 14 action dimensions, chunk size 50 and 10 denoising steps, and no measurements from running the policy on all five GPUs. On B100, raising denoising steps from 10 to 50 raises total latency 2.15×; raising chunk size from 50 to 250 raises it 11% <Cite id="vla-perf-2026" />. [Real-Time Execution](/manipulation/realtime-execution) develops these latency budgets.

<Image id="jetson-agx-orin-auledas-2024" />

These batch-one analytical predictions use the 2.7B π0 baseline with 3 cameras, 14 action dimensions, chunk size 50 and 10 denoising steps, without measuring the policy on all five GPUs. On B100, raising denoising steps from 10 to 50 raises total latency 2.15×; raising chunk size from 50 to 250 raises it 11% <Cite id="vla-perf-2026" />. [Real-Time Execution](/manipulation/realtime-execution) develops these latency budgets.
